Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let $H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form $\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ $$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$ This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is $\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$. Thus its Weyl unitary is $W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$, $$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$ For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is $$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$ Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and two-point function $$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$ which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields. The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is $$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$ understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance. For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and for the bounded Weyl operators. For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector $(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions. No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and use the definitions in [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. For every $\mu\ge0$ and almost every $\mathbf k$, the displayed Pauli blocks satisfy $h_D(\mathbf k)^\dagger=h_D(\mathbf k)$, $h_D(\mathbf k)^2=\omega(\mathbf k)^2I_4$, and $P_\pm(\mathbf k)$ are complementary orthogonal projections of rank two. The ranges $\mathcal H_\pm$ are closed separable Hilbert subspaces of $\mathcal H_D$, and $h_D$ is self-adjoint on $D(h_D)=\{u:\omega u\in\mathcal H_D\}$. The matrices also satisfy $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ and $\gamma^{0\dagger}=\gamma^0$, $\gamma^{j\dagger}=-\gamma^j$. For a unit spatial vector $\mathbf n$, put $\Sigma_{\mathbf n}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n)$, $S_R(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)I_4-i\sin(\theta/2)\Sigma_{\mathbf n}$, and $S_B(\chi)=\cosh(\chi/2)I_4+\sinh(\chi/2)\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf n$. With $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$ the rotation $\mathbf v_\parallel+\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_\perp+\sin\theta\,\mathbf n\times\mathbf v_\perp$ using [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], with $\mathbf v_\parallel=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n$ and $\mathbf v_\perp=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_\parallel$, and $B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)$ the boost defined in [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]], these matrices satisfy $S_R\Gamma(p)S_R^{-1}=\Gamma(R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)p)$, $S_B\Gamma(p)S_B^{-1}=\Gamma(B_{\mathbf n}(\chi)p)$, and $S_R\beta S_R^\dagger=S_B\beta S_B^\dagger=\beta$. For each real $t$, $W_D(t,\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] is unitary, satisfies $W_D(t+s,\mathbf k)=W_D(t,\mathbf k)W_D(s,\mathbf k)$, and obeys $\partial_tW_D(t,\mathbf k)=i h_D(\mathbf k)W_D(t,\mathbf k)$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps $c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set $$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$ Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces, $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy $$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$ The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space $$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$ This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does not assign particle statistics to a physical species.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

derivations.claim: The measure $d\nu_\mu$ is sigma-finite by [F9], and $\omega_\mu$ and $k_j$ are finite measurable multipliers by [F2]. Applying [F5] with one-particle multiplier vector $(1,\omega_\mu,-k_1,-k_2,-k_3)$ gives the self-adjoint scalar operators $N_s,H_s,P_{s,j}$. On sector $n$, their multipliers are $n$, $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, and $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$. Squaring these multipliers and integrating against the completed product measure yields exactly the stated domains.

The Dirac data in [F6] satisfy the measurable, finite-multiplier hypotheses of [F7], and [F16] supplies the complementary orthogonal projections and closed ranges required by that carrier. The one-particle measure is sigma-finite: each of the two species copies of R^3 is the countable union of bounded balls with finite Lebesgue measure. Let Y_m be the two species copies restricted to the ball of radius m; each Y_m has finite measure. For fixed n, the product sets Y_m^n have finite product measure and cover X^n as m grows. Their countable union over n and m is a sigma-finite cover of the Fock direct-sum measure. The particle and antiparticle sector multipliers are therefore self-adjoint on the maximal domains in [F7], which are the displayed square-integrability conditions for $H_D$ and each $P_{D,j}$. The field boundedness and equal-time CAR are exactly the inspected interfaces in [F8].

For real $f$, [F3] identifies the scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ with $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$. The Hilbert space $H_\mu$ is separable by [F13], so the hypothesis of the Segal-domain result [F4] holds. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar $\sqrt2$ does not change an operator domain; hence the closure is self-adjoint on the domain in [F4] with $h=K_\mu f$. If $K_\mu f=0$, both operators are zero on all Fock space.

For a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $|\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle|\le\|A\Psi\|<\infty$. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, this expectation is real. The vector $A\Psi-\langle A\rangle_\Psi\Psi$ belongs to the Hilbert space because both terms do, so its norm and the stated variance are finite without requiring $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. By [F14], a product $AB$ acts only on vectors $\Psi\in D(B)$ for which $B\Psi\in D(A)$; it is not defined merely because both $A$ and $B$ separately exist on a common dense core.

Choose $b_d$ from [F18] for $d=3,4$. Put
$Z_d=\int b_d(x)\,d^dx$ and $\rho_d=Z_d^{-1}b_d$.
The integral is finite because $0\le b_d\le1$ and its support lies in a
bounded ball, and it is positive because $b_d=1$ on a ball of positive
volume. Every derivative of $b_d$ is continuous with compact support, so
all its coordinate-weighted derivatives are bounded. Thus $\rho_d$ is
Schwartz, nonnegative, nonzero, and has integral one. In particular
$0<\|\rho_d\|_2<\infty$. Define
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\rho_d(x)\,d^dx$.
The integral triangle inequality gives $|\widehat\rho_d(\xi)|\le\int\rho_d=1$;
dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\rho_d$, gives
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)\to1$ as $\xi\to0$.
Set $\rho=\rho_4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)=\varepsilon^{-4}\rho_4((x-x_0)/\varepsilon)$. For every Schwartz test $\phi$, change of variables and dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\|\phi\|_\infty\rho_4(y)$, give $\int\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$, so this is a point-mass approximation. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in H_\mu^+$ the same change of variables gives
$$K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)=e^{ip\circ x_0}\widehat\rho_4\bigl(\varepsilon(-p^0,\mathbf p)\bigr).$$
Thus $K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for every fixed shell momentum and $|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)|\le1$. The shell measure has infinite total mass: in radial coordinates, for $r\ge\max(1,\mu)$, $\omega_\mu(r)\le\sqrt2\,r$, so its radial density is bounded below by a positive constant times $r\,dr$, whose integral diverges. Fatou's lemma [F11] therefore gives $\liminf_{\varepsilon_m\downarrow0}\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|^2\ge\int_{H_\mu^+}1\,d\nu_\mu=\infty$. By [F1, F3] and the creation formula on the vacuum, $\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0})\Omega\|=\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|$, so these vacuum vectors have no finite-norm point-field limit.

The scalar one-particle space contains a unit vector $e$, for example a normalized indicator of an annulus $1<|\mathbf k|<2$, whose shell measure is finite and positive by [F2]. The symmetric vectors $e^{\otimes n}$ are unit vectors in mutually orthogonal sectors. Put $C=(\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4})^{-1/2}$ and $\Psi_n=Cn^{-2}e^{\otimes n}$. By [F15], $\sum n^{-4}$ converges and is positive, so $C$ is well-defined and $\Psi$ is normalized. Also by [F15], $\sum n^{-2}<\infty$, so $\Psi\in D(N_s)$ and $N_s\Psi=(Cn^{-1}e^{\otimes n})_{n\ge1}$ is a Fock vector. Its image under one more application of $N_s$ would have squared norm $C^2\sum_{n\ge1}1=\infty$, so $N_s\Psi\notin D(N_s)$. By the composition-domain rule [F14] with $A=B=N_s$, $\Psi\notin D(N_s^2)$. Its mean and variance are finite by 2.2.

Fix a unit spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\rho_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\varepsilon)z$. For every spatial Schwartz test, change of variables and [F10] show that its pairing with $u_\varepsilon$ tends to the test's value at $\mathbf x_0$ times $z$, while $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2=\varepsilon^{-3/2}\|\rho_3\|_2\to\infty$. By [F16], choose countable dense sets in the two Dirac energy ranges. Conjugating the negative-range dense set preserves density, and the Cartesian product of the two dense sets is countable and dense in the Hilbert direct sum. Therefore the one-particle space for the CAR Fock representation is separable and [F17] applies. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. The adjoint identity swaps $x$ and $y$, so the same two-vector supremum equals $\|A_\varepsilon^\dagger\|$. For bounded operators $X,Y$, each unit $\xi$ satisfies $\|XY\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\|$ and $\|(X+Y)\xi\|\le\|X\xi\|+\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|+\|Y\|$; taking suprema gives product submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality. Applying these inequalities to the CAR identity yields $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon\|\le2\|A_\varepsilon\|^2$. Thus $\|A_\varepsilon\|\ge\|u_\varepsilon\|_2/\sqrt2\to\infty$, excluding a bounded equal-time point-field norm limit.

Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.
